podcast.title: Aer Lingus Air Rage Arrest and Bipolar Diagnosis (2014-2016)
podcast.body: On November 10, 2014, Dolores O'Riordan was arrested after a disturbance on Aer Lingus flight 110 from New York to Shannon, about 20 minutes before landing. She was described as irrational and aggressive, injuring a flight attendant, headbutting a police officer, and resisting arrest while proclaiming, "I'm an icon. I'm the queen of Limerick." Transferred to St. Patrick's Psychiatric Hospital, she was diagnosed with bipolar disorder, paranoid and delusional, and stayed for three weeks. She pleaded guilty in December 2015 and was fined $6,600 Canadian on February 24, 2016, with the judge noting her mental illness. The episode was attributed to stress, sleep deprivation, recent separation from her husband of 21 years, and the second anniversary of her father's death. "Dolores has since been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and the stress and sleep deprivation she'd been under triggered an episode."

podcast.title: Resisting Arrest and Psychiatric Evaluation (2014)
podcast.body: Following the Aer Lingus incident, Dolores O'Riordan did not go quietly, resisting arrest with defiant statements like, "You can't arrest me. I'm an icon. I'm the queen of Lerick." Described as "quite irrational, quite aggressive, quite difficult," she banged and kicked in the patrol car, headbutted a chasing cop after escaping, and continued singing and shouting in jail before being transferred to St. Patrick's Psychiatric Hospital for a three-week stay and a diagnosis of being "genuinely mentally ill, paranoid and delusional." podcast.title: Guilty Plea and Bipolar Disorder Diagnosis (2015-2016)
podcast.body: In December 2015, Dolores O'Riordan pleaded guilty to charges of air rage, stating she had no memory of the events but did not deny her involvement. She was subsequently diagnosed with bipolar disorder, with the episode attributed to hypomania triggered by stress and sleep deprivation, exacerbated by her recent separation from her husband of 21 years, the second anniversary of her father's death, and weeks away from her children while living out of a suitcase. On February 24, 2016, she was fined $6,600 Canadian, with the judge noting it would be unfair to be harsher given her mental illness. "She was diagnosed as being genuinely mentally ill, paranoid and delusional."

podcast.title: Death at London Hilton (January 15, 2018)
podcast.body: Dolores O'Riordan died in room 2005 at the London Hilton on Park Lane in Mayfair on January 15, 2018. She had flown from New York to London to work on a solo project titled "Dark" and discuss a new Cranberries album. At 1:12 am, she left an enthusiastic voicemail for a friend about the recording progress, and at 2:00 am, she called her mother, with things appearing fine. She was later found submerged in her bathtub, with numerous empty mini-bar alcohol bottles, an empty champagne bottle, and prescription pills in the room. Toxicology reports indicated that drugs were not an issue, but her blood alcohol content at the time of death was 0.33, more than four times the legal limit for drunk driving. Her death was ruled as accidental drowning due to alcohol toxicity. She was 46. "Dolores or Reardon of the Cranberries... found her submerged in the bathtub."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discovery and Official Report (January 15, 2018 - September 16, 2018)
podcast.body: Dolores O'Riordan was discovered at approximately 9 AM on January 15, 2018, by a maid who came to tidy the room, found face up in the tub with water covering her mouth and nose. Police were called, CPR was performed, but she was declared dead at 9:16 AM at the age of 46. The final report on her death, released on September 16, 2018 (which would have been her 47th birthday), concluded that she died from accidental drowning due to alcohol intoxication, with no suicide note found and rumors of fentanyl involvement disproven. "She was found at about 9 in the morning of January 15th by a maid who had come to tidy up. She was face up in the tub with the water covering her mouth and nose."

podcast.title: Last Communications (January 14-15, 2018)
podcast.body: On Sunday, January 14, 2018, she emailed The Cranberries guitarist, Noel Hogan, sketches of new songs. At 1:12 AM on January 15, she left a slurred voicemail for her friend Dan Waite, a label executive, expressing great optimism about her life, including a new house and furniture shopping; this voicemail is historically recognized as her final recording. At 3 AM, she spoke to her mother, which was the last time anyone heard from her. "At 1.12am on the morning of the 15th, she left a slurry voicemail for her friend Dan Wait, a labeled executive, saying that she felt very good about everything, including a new house that involved shopping for some furniture."

podcast.title: Bipolar Disorder Diagnosis
podcast.body: A couple of years after her airplane incident, Dolores O'Riordan admitted she had bipolar disorder and was receiving medication. This diagnosis provided context for earlier band issues like tour cancellations and internal disagreements. "un par de años más tarde acaba asmitiendo que tenía otra estornada bipolar porque estaba medicado y entonces como que empezabas a entender muchas cosas que había pasado en la banda tanto cancelaciones como discusiones entre ellos."

podcast.title: Cause of Death
podcast.body: While the exact cause of her death remains unconfirmed, it is believed to have been from natural causes, possibly an infarct or an embolism, which helped prevent sensationalism. "por lo que dicen parece que haya sido una causa natural como puede ser un infarto o un embolia entonces tampoco gracias a Dios no va a dar especulaciones ni asensacionalismo."

podcast.title: Circumstances of Death
podcast.body: After her final call, Dolores O'Riordan drew a bath and consumed the contents of the minibar, including five small bottles of spirits and one bottle of champagne. A prescription for the sedative lorazepam was found in her room, though an autopsy later confirmed that the levels in her blood were not excessive. Wearing a long-sleeved vest and pajama bottoms, she entered the tub, became drowsy from the alcohol, slipped beneath the water, and drowned. "She was made sleepy by all the alcohol. She slipped below the surface of the water, and she drowned."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Delicate Health and False Rumors
podcast.body: Dolores O'Riordan's health was consistently delicate throughout her career, leading to various cancellations and speculation. False rumors circulated in the early 2000s claiming she had cancer or heart problems, with the band sometimes offering unconvincing explanations like back issues. "su salud siempre había sido bastante delicada ... se va a decir que ella tenía cáncer a primeros del 2000, se dijo que tenía problemas de corazón ellos tampoco nos daban historias muy convicentes a veces decían que tenía problemas espalda."

podcast.title: Iconic Status and Collaborations
podcast.body: In her final 15 years, Dolores O'Riordan became a charismatic icon, despite her band's dissolution and her solo career not achieving major chart success. She collaborated with numerous prominent artists, including Bono, Pavarotti, Supero, and Mick Jagger. "se ya se convertió como un icono carismático al final tenemos grabaciones de esta mujer cantando con bono, contando con paparotica, cantando con supero, cantando con muchísima gente con Mick Jagger."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Personal Struggles and Relocation
podcast.body: Dolores O'Riordan faced recurring issues with alcohol and experienced the breakup of her 20-year marriage. Following her divorce, she left Balgonie, Ontario, where she had lived with her Canadian husband, and eventually settled in New York, first at Trump Tower and then in the East Village. "There were reoccurring issues with alcohol. Her marriage broke up after 20 years. She left Bacorn, Ontario, where she'd been living with her Canadian husband and eventually settled in New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Physical Health Issues
podcast.body: O'Riordan also suffered from a slipped disc in her back, caused by picking up a guitar, which caused enough pain to force the cancellation of a tour. "There was at least one other health problem. A slipped disc in her back caused by picking up a guitar, and that hurt enough for one tour to be canceled."

podcast.title: Suicide Note Attempt and Mental Health
podcast.body: On a night in September 2017, Dolores O'Riordan took sedatives, drank heavily, and began writing a suicide note, though she ultimately abandoned it. Her psychotherapist, assigned to her, reportedly did not express concern that she might attempt a similar act again. "And on a night in September 2017, she took some sedatives and started drinking heavily and began to write a suicide note."

xref.title: Andy Rourke Death (May 18, 2023) – Pancreatic Cancer, Age 59; Sued Morrissey, Later Played Two Morrissey Singles
xref.body: Andy Rourke was a founding member of the Smiths and is considered by fans one of the greatest bassists in the history of British indie rock. His time with the band ended badly: a heroin addiction, a lawsuit against Morrissey and Johnny Marr for unpaid royalties (he was broke), and a decade later a bankruptcy over tax issues. Post-Smiths, he worked with the Pretenders, Killing Joke, Stone Roses singer Ian Brown, Dolores O'Riordan and the Cranberries, and Peter Hook of New Order. In a remarkable reconciliation, he played on two Morrissey solo singles despite the money disputes. His father and sister were both diagnosed with cancer, which prompted him to start a cancer charity; he himself was later diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. He died in a New York hospital on May 18, 2023, age 59. "Ask any Smiths fan, and they'll tell you that he was one of the greatest bassists in the history of British Indie Rock."

xref.title: Dolores O'Riordan's Approval and Tragic Death
xref.body: Dolores O'Riordan, lead singer of The Cranberries, not only loved Bad Wolves' version of "Zombie" but offered to join them in London to add guitar or background vocals, leaving an excited voice message the night before the planned session. Tragically, she was found dead the next morning, January 15, 2018, having passed out in a bath after heavy drinking. "At the night before, she left a voice message, saying how excited she was about the project, and that she'd see everybody the next day."

xref.title: Dolores O'Riordan's Global Fame and Struggles
xref.body: For a period, Dolores O'Riordan was one of the most famous singers worldwide. However, the immense pressure of the music business, continuous touring, and constant harassment from tabloids and paparazzi led her to suffer a nervous breakdown at the age of 24. She lived a "delicate existence" thereafter, eventually dying in a London hotel room at 46. "And for a while, she was one of the most famous singers in the entire world, male or female. But that didn't work well with her."

xref.title: Dolores O'Riordan's Impact
xref.body: Dolores O'Riordan, the face and voice of The Cranberries, possessed a powerful and unique vocal style, recognized as one of the most distinctive in the history of alternative rock. She was a significant influence on contemporary artists like Adele, Florence Welch, and Halsey. "Her powerful vocal style was unique and has been called one of the most distinctive voices in the history of Al Rock. Talk to Adele or Florence Welcher, Hallsley, and they'll tell you that Dolores was a huge influence on them."

xref.title: Unique Identity and Influences
xref.body: Halsey has synthesized various influences, including Jagger, Bowie, Amy Winehouse, and Dolores O'Riordan, to craft a distinctive identity. This identity incorporates concepts of gender identity, bisexuality, film noir, mental health, political activism, racial justice, and motherhood, all stemming from an authentic personal place. "Halsey has taken a bunch of different influences from Jagger and Bowie to Amy Winehouse and Dolores are reared in and crafted a unique identity that also includes concepts of gender identity, bisexuality, film noir, mental health, political activism, racial justice, motherhood, and so much more."
